description: Higía is a team based in Buenos Aires participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are developing health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions, featuring clear health indicators, interactive visualizations, and practical guidelines to help assess and maintain astronaut health during long-duration space missions.
summary:
Tesai is a health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration space missions, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It combines a crew health twin, cabin-environment monitoring, private daily check-ins, and a helmet-visor interface that guides the crew through emergencies.

The project addresses the challenge of protecting crew health when communication with Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way. Tesai displays vital signs, sleep, activity, CO2, oxygen, pressure, temperature, humidity, and radiation. Each value is compared with reference ranges and the astronaut’s personal baseline. An evidence button shows whether a threshold comes from a published source, was adapted, or was a team design decision.

Tesai includes an immersive first-person simulation with three emergencies: a Mars EVA, a pressurized rover, and a spacecraft in transit. In each scenario, the user acts as the first responder and receives step-by-step guidance, voice alerts, and a simulated Earth link to escalate unacknowledged critical situations.

The system reduces false alarms through persistence checks, noise filtering, and sensor-failure separation. Daily check-ins remain on the device and never generate alerts or shared reports, encouraging honest self-reporting. Tesai is important because it turns health data into trustworthy, contextualized, and actionable information, helping crews make safer decisions when immediate medical support is unavailable.
details:
Tesai is a browser-based health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It combines a crew health twin, cabin-environment monitoring, private daily check-ins, views of the wearable devices crews use, and a helmet-visor interface that guides the crew through emergencies.

How it works
Tesai shows vital signs, sleep, activity, and cabin conditions including CO₂, oxygen, pressure, temperature, humidity, and radiation. Each reading is compared with reference ranges and the astronaut’s personal baseline. An evidence panel explains whether each threshold comes from a published source, was adapted, or was a team design decision, with the sources in APA format.

By default the app replays real public data: heart rate, heart rate variability and sleep from healthy adults (PhysioNet MMASH and a small BIDSleep sample; they are not astronauts), and real ISS cabin temperature, humidity and CO₂ from NASA OSDR. Metrics those datasets do not measure show “no data”. A simulated source is available for demos.

The project includes an immersive first-person simulation with three emergency scenarios: a Mars EVA, a pressurized rover, and a spacecraft in transit. Users act as the first responder, receive step-by-step guidance from a “second doctor”, and can activate voice alerts and a simulated delay-tolerant Earth link. The Biometrics view also shows signal quality and isometric, separable drawings of real wearables (Bio-Monitor, ARCHeR, BioButton, Triggerfish contact lens and a dosimeter badge).

Benefits and impact
Tesai is designed to improve situational awareness, make health data easier to trust, support faster emergency response, and encourage honest self-reporting. The daily check-in stays on the device and does not generate alerts or shared reports. Persistence checks, noise filtering, and sensor-failure separation are designed to reduce false alarms. Its intended impact is to make space health monitoring more transparent, human-centered, and actionable for crews far from immediate medical support.

Technology and design
Tesai was built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript ES modules, and SVG. The 3D simulation uses Three.js (loaded from a CDN), Web Speech API provides voice guidance, and Web Audio generates alert tones. It needs no build step, framework, npm installation, server, or database; it is served as static files. Small Python scripts convert the public datasets once, before deployment.

The team considered accessibility, bilingual English-Spanish support, privacy, data provenance, alert fatigue, communication delays, and the ethical limits of a non-diagnostic prototype. The check-in history and the simulation scenarios are simulated. Tesai is not a medical device. Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Bob helped build it; no AI runs inside the app. The code is released under the MIT license.
